text: A bank's favorite number led its workers to open three and a half million fake accounts.
It's Wells Fargo, one of the biggest banks in America, and its favorite number is eight.
Why eight? Because, the boss once wrote to shareholders, eight rhymed with great.
Every branch got targets, and every worker got a daily number.
Hit it, and you got a bonus. Miss it, and you heard about it.
So workers started opening accounts for customers who never asked.
They ordered debit cards, made up PINs, and even invented email addresses.
One card here, one account there. Every single day.
In twenty sixteen, regulators reported two million accounts nobody had asked for, and fifty three hundred workers were fired.
Luckily, thousands of customers got brand new credit cards. Unluckily, some of them also got the fees.
Why did it happen? Pay a kid for every weed he pulls, and soon he starts planting weeds.
When the number becomes the goal, people stop chasing the goal and start chasing the number.
The bank agreed to pay three billion dollars, and the government banned it from getting any bigger.
So for seven years, the bank that wanted eight of everything wasn't allowed to grow.
